description: Draft library of small experiments a participant can try, one or two per behavior. Written for the participant ('you'). Content for a researcher to review and edit; the selection code in experiments.ts picks from it.

experiments.title: Ask five people what you are best at
experiments.why: It is hard to see your own strengths. People who have worked with you can tell you what you do better than most and what to avoid, which is a better starting point for choosing roles than job titles.
steps: List the work from the past few years that gave you energy and the work that drained you.
Pick five people who have seen your work: a former manager, peers, someone you mentored, a friend who knows your field.
Ask each: what do I do better than most people, what would you trust me with, and what should I avoid or get help with?
Look for what at least three people said, and compare it with your own list.
Write three strengths to build your target around and two kinds of work to avoid.
experiments.effort: About 20 minutes of reflection and five 15-minute conversations
experiments.track: The strengths and things to avoid that more than one person named, and whether your target follows from them.

experiments.title: Write your target on one page
experiments.why: A target you have written down is easier to hold on to when a tempting but off-target role appears.
steps: List the role, level, industry, type of company, location or work setting, pay, and the kind of work you want.
Mark each item Must-have or Flexible, and write one line on why.
Identify 10-20 target companies that you would like to join.
Keep the page where you search, and read it before you apply.
experiments.track: Whether you can say in one sentence why each role you apply to fits your page.

experiments.title: Build a routine for finding roles early
experiments.why: Roles that match your target are often posted in a few specific places. A routine that brings them to you, plus a quick written check of each one, saves time and keeps you from drifting off target.
steps: Turn your target into search terms: titles, keywords, location, level, and pay if the site allows it.
Set up alerts or saved searches on two or three job sites, and add sources specific to your field, such as niche boards, newsletters, or communities.
List 15 to 20 companies you would like to work for and follow their career pages.
Check your alerts once a day. For each role, write one line against your one-page target: strong match, partial, or stretch, one reason you are credible, one real gap, and apply or pass.
Apply to your strongest-fit roles within a couple of days of posting, and each week note which source surfaced your best-fit roles.
experiments.effort: About 45 minutes to set up, then 10 to 15 minutes a day
experiments.track: How old roles are when you apply, the share that are a strong match, and which source surfaces the best-fit roles.

experiments.title: Lead with two reasons to interview you
experiments.why: A reader should be able to see why you fit within the first few seconds, without hunting for it.
steps: For a priority role, write the two or three reasons the hiring team should interview you.
Put those reasons in the top third of your resume or in the first lines of your summary.
Attach one concrete result to each reason, such as a number, a scale, or an outcome.
Cut or shorten one thing that does not support those reasons.
experiments.track: Whether tailored applications get more responses than ones you send unchanged.

experiments.title: Match your time to the opportunity
experiments.why: Putting your best effort where it counts leaves you free to move quickly on roles that are less likely to lead anywhere.
steps: Sort roles into A (strong fit and you want it), B (reasonable fit), and C (a stretch).
Give A roles your full effort, for example 45 to 60 minutes with tailoring and research.
Give B roles a lighter pass of 15 to 20 minutes, and either skip C roles or send them with minimal effort.
Keep the same tiers for two weeks before changing them.
experiments.effort: Reshuffles your time rather than adding to it
experiments.track: How many applications you send at each tier, and the responses from each.

experiments.title: Use AI to prepare, check what it writes, and keep the decisions yourself
experiments.why: AI is useful for research and drafting, but it can add or exaggerate. Checking its output against your own record, and deciding yourself what to apply to and what to claim, keeps the speed without the risk.
steps: Ask an AI tool for a one-page brief on the company and the role.
Paste in the posting and your resume and ask it to list the gaps.
Decide yourself which gaps matter and what to emphasize.
Before you submit anything AI wrote or changed, read it top to bottom and check every claim and number against your source resume. Remove anything it added or exaggerated.
Do not let any tool submit applications for you.
experiments.effort: About 10 minutes of preparation and 5 minutes of checking per priority role
experiments.track: Whether the research changes what you apply to or how you position yourself, and how often your check finds something to fix.

experiments.title: Look for a human path before you apply to a priority role
experiments.why: A role where someone knows who you are before or soon after you apply gives your application a better chance of being read.
steps: Search for former colleagues, shared connections, or employees at the company.
Find the recruiter or hiring manager if you can.
Send a short, specific note about why the role interests you.
Apply either way.
experiments.track: How many priority roles had a human contact, and how those responded compared with ones without.

experiments.title: Ask for advice first, not for a job
experiments.why: Asking for a referral on a first call can feel transactional to both people. Asking for perspective is an easy yes, and it often leads naturally to introductions.
steps: Pick three people connected to roles or companies you want.
Ask for 15 minutes to hear how their team works and what you should know.
Near the end, ask: who else should I talk to?
Within two days, send a short thank-you that mentions one thing you learned.
Only later, when it fits, mention a role you are considering.
experiments.effort: About 15 minutes per conversation, three conversations
experiments.track: Conversations held, introductions received, and follow-ups sent.

experiments.title: Rewrite your profile for the role you want
experiments.why: Recruiters search by role and skills, then skim a headline and a few lines. A profile written for the role you want gets found and understood faster than one that lists every job you have had.
steps: Write a headline that names the role you want, not your current title.
Rewrite the first lines of your summary around that role and two or three results you are proud of.
Match the skills list and location to the roles you are targeting, and turn on the setting that tells recruiters you are open to work if that fits your situation.
Ask one person who hires for that role to read it for 30 seconds and tell you what they took away.
experiments.effort: About an hour, plus one short conversation
experiments.track: Recruiter messages and profile views in the two weeks before and after the change.

experiments.title: Keep a simple tracker
experiments.why: You cannot see what is working without a record of where each application came from and what happened.
steps: Make a sheet with columns for date, role, source, time spent, response, and outcome.
Fill it in as you apply, in under a minute.
Once a week, spend 10 minutes counting responses and interviews by source.
Use email Inbox to track each application.
experiments.effort: About one minute per application, plus 10 minutes a week

experiments.title: Move one block of time toward what is working
experiments.why: If one path produces more conversations for you, giving it more of your time is a low-risk way to test whether that continues.
steps: Look at where your responses and interviews have come from.
Pick one block of time each week, for example two hours, and move it to the source that works best.
Keep this up for two weeks.
Compare responses before and after.
experiments.track: Responses and conversations per week, before and after.

experiments.title: Run one two-week experiment
experiments.why: Changing one thing at a time, and deciding in advance how you will judge it, tells you whether the change helped.
steps: Pick one change, such as a new type of outreach message or a different resume top line.
Write down what you expect to happen and the number you will check.
Try it consistently for two weeks.
At the end, compare the result with your expectation, then keep it or drop it.
After any recruiter screen, ask for one piece of feedback.
experiments.effort: A few minutes of planning, then your normal search
experiments.track: The one number you chose in step 2.
